newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE - Euro spurs Japan's drive for global yen.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Euro spurs Japan's drive for global yen.

text.p: The planned launch of a single European currency in 1999 is spurring Japan's drive to boost the yen's role as an international currency, but the road to a global yen looks like being anything but smooth.
"The euro (single European currency) is among our motives for more aggressive financial deregulation, which would in turn help raise the yen's status," said a Finance Ministry official.
The future will see a new tripolar currency order and the yen should rank with the euro and the dollar, he told Reuters.
With that in mind, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto last November announced a "Big Bang" plan to open up Japan's financial markets by 2001, the official added.
Tokyo also wants to boost the yen's global role to stem the flow of the country's wealth out of yen into foreign currencies.
Japan is the world's largest creditor nation with its overseas assets exceeding $750 billion dollars, most of which is denominated in the U.S. currency.

"Japan has lost much of the country's wealth, which has gone into foreign currency assets because the yen has remained merely a local currency," said C.H. Kwan, a senior economist at Nomura Research Institute's Center for Policy Research.

"Japan's policy challenge is to create an environment which encourages a wider use of the yen not just to achieve equality with the euro and the dollar but to protect the wealth of a nation which is ageing at an unprecedented speed," Kwan said.
ROCKY ROAD AHEAD
But analysts say there are some difficult hurdles to clear to boost the yen's global prestige, including ensuring Japan's economy achieves sustainable growth.
"The euro will definitely outperform the yen if things remain as they are now," said Hal Deguchi, general manager of Nippon Life Insurance Co's international planning department.
The status of a currency depended on a country's committment to reform itself to achieve sustainable economic growth.
"In this regard, the yen's status is already under a threat," Deguchi said.

Europe's Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) is due to start on January 1, 1999, with the creation of the European Central Bank (ECB) and the introduction of a single currency, although not all members of the bloc are sure to join it on that date.
"But Europeans are at least steering in a direction which would undoubtedly add to the strength of the currency, such as their struggle towards meeting the EMU's tough budget criteria," Deguchi said.
"The dollar's role as the world's key currency will remain unchanged after the launch of the euro," said Taisuke Tanaka, a market strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston's Tokyo branch.
The yen might benefit from an initially unstable euro as investors seek a safe haven but could quickly fade back to its status as "the world's largest local currency", Tanaka said.
"Free, liquid financial markets and solid economic growth in Japan may come only after the launch of Euro," he added.
FINANCE MINISTRY FOREX POLICY AND THE BIG BANG
The boost to the yen's global role from the "Big Bang" would also be undermined if Japan pursued the same policy of favouring a weak yen as it has in the past, analysts said.

"Any positive impact from the "Big Bang' on the yen will be more than neutralised if the government sticks to a weak yen policy that is already prompting sales of yen assets and blocking more use of the yen," Deguchi said.
While some policy makers have been lamenting the yen's latest slide, Hashimoto greeted the dollar's rise to the 118 yen level by telling reporters the yen's weakness was not necessarily excessive.
Forex policymakers at the finance ministry had vigorously pursued a weak yen policy over the past several years while the yen soared to a historic high of 79.75 yen to a dollar.
Japan spent an estimated $64.73 billion in efforts to rein in the galloping yen in the two years to last December.

The Trade Ministry said the weak yen trend had sliced the ratio of Japanese trade denominated in yen to a seven-year low of 35.2 percent last September, down from the peak of 42.8 percent in March 1993.
JAPAN'S BUDGET BALANCE
Japan's half-hearted attempt at tackling its bloated public sector deficit is another drag on the yen's global prestige.

The Tokyo stock market has nose-dived of late in response to market pessimism sparked by a proposed budget for the business year from April, which the government describes as aimed at getting the country's big budget deficit under control.

But while the growth in general expenditures in 1997/98 budget will be restrained, the overall size will grow almost 10 percent over the initial 1996/97 budget due to rises in debt-servicing costs and grants to municipal governments.

European countries wanting to join the EMU must cut their public debt to three percent or less of gross domestic product to do so. Japan has set a similar target for reducing state and local government debt -- now about six percent of GDP -- but has set the years 2005/6 as the deadline for doing so.
CHANGE IN FUTURE?

Still, despite the doubts over Hashimoto's reform plans and the prospect of a greater global role for the yen, some bureaucrats appear ready to make the necessary drastic changes, including altering anachronistic tax and accounting rules.

Analysts say accounting standards need to be brought in line with global standards and the securities transaction tax, which raises the cost of trading securities here, should be abolished to improve Tokyo market liquidity -- a key to increasing the proportion of business conducted in yen.
"Looking back on history, all the drastic changes in this country have come abruptly after a crisis," Deguchi said.
